items.title: Jack Teagarden Interview, 1959-10-29
items.q: There was a little kid with us, uh, the name of Benny Goodman. In those days he was about 18 years old. Jimmy McPartland and, uh, Bud Freeman.

ctx.x: Okay, whenever you're ready. Well, how did you learn trombone and develop your style? That's what I really like to know.

Well, I'll tell you, when I was, uh, pretty young, my mother and I used to play in, uh, the old silent movie theaters. We used to play for the comedies and, uh, I don't know, just trombone and piano. You know, learn more technique because I had the whole, swing the whole thing, melody and all. You know. And, uh, my mother played very good ragtime piano, which was very good for those years. Then, uh, I lost my father in 1918 with the flu. And then I went, we went to Oklahoma City. And I went one more year of, uh,…

Can we back up for a minute and go back to your early period? Yeah. Because there's some particular people I'd like to ask you about some particular things. What kind of training did Peg Kelly have that he should develop this wonderful style?

items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: In fact, I recorded with Jack just before he died. He hired me for the record date.

ctx.x: Oh, yes, in a glass; he was a great natural talent. And Teagarden could read anything you know, he played in the Whiteman band where you and we had to read some heavy stuff. Well, anyway, Oh, I wanted to say about Teagarden that although we were good friends and he seemed to like me very much, musically and... we got along reasonably.

In fact, I recorded with Jack just before he died. He hired me for the record date. And I think the sad thing about his life, or maybe it wasn't a sad thing, was that he never, although he enjoyed listening to intelligent people talk about the theatre or books, he never got into that himself. He was not what one would call a social kind of man.
